articles.title: Insulin Dose-Adjusted Hemoglobin A1c Has Suboptimal Performance for Identifying C-Peptide-Defined Partial Remission: The SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth Study.
articles.abstract: Insulin dose-adjusted hemoglobin A1c (IDAA1c = HbA1c [%] + [4 × total daily dose in units/kg/day]) ≤9 is widely used to define partial remission in pediatric type 1 diabetes and as an eligibility criterion or outcome in disease-modifying therapy trials. However, it has not been validated in U.S. youth. Because higher BMI increases insulin resistance and insulin requirements, we hypothesized that IDAA1c would perform suboptimally in participants with overweight or obesity. We analyzed data from 422 SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth study participants with mixed-meal tolerance test (MMTT)-stimulated C-peptide within 12 months of diagnosis. Partial remission was defined using MMTT-stimulated area under the curve (AUC) mean C-peptide. Participant characteristics were compared by BMI category (<85th percentile [normal or underweight] and ≥85th percentile [overweight or obese]) using Wilcoxon rank sum and Fisher exact tests. Sensitivity, specificity, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) AUC of IDAA1c ≤9 for identifying partial remission were evaluated. Participants with normal or underweight versus participants with overweight or obesity had lower IDAA1c (8.95 vs. 9.28, P = 0.043) despite lower stimulated C-peptide (1.25 vs. 1.88 ng/mL, P < 0.001). Overall, IDAA1c ≤9 had 61% sensitivity and 79% specificity for predicting C-peptide ≥0.91 ng/mL with an ROC AUC of 0.77. Among participants with overweight or obesity, sensitivity was 45% and specificity 81%. A Youden index-derived cutoff of IDAA1c ≤11.6 improved sensitivity to 93%, with specificity of 54% in participants with overweight or obesity. IDAA1c ≤9 demonstrated suboptimal accuracy as a screening test for partial remission, especially underestimating β-cell function in youth with overweight or obesity. BMI-specific cutoffs improved sensitivity but reduced specificity.

articles.title: Intraoperative Dobutamine Plus Norepinephrine to Prevent Postoperative Acute Kidney Injury in Septic Shock: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: International guidelines recommend dobutamine for management of septic shock and cardiac dysfunction with persistent hypoperfusion in adults based on very low-certainty evidence. Randomized trials are lacking on the effect of intraoperative dobutamine combined with norepinephrine vs norepinephrine on postoperative outcomes in patients with septic shock undergoing surgical source control. To determine whether intraoperative dobutamine combined with norepinephrine reduces acute kidney injury (AKI) within 7 postoperative days in patients with septic shock undergoing surgical source control. This randomized, open-label clinical trial in 39 tertiary hospitals in China enrolled adults with septic shock who were undergoing surgical source control between June 2024 and August 2025. Follow-up ended on November 15, 2025. Intraoperative, intravenous infusion of dobutamine (up to 5 µg/kg/min) combined with norepinephrine vs norepinephrine alone. The primary outcome was new-onset AKI or worsening of preoperative AKI within 7 days after surgery, defined using Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) criteria. The 11 secondary outcomes included Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score on postoperative day 1 and urine output 1 hour post intervention. Among 584 patients (median [IQR] age, 67.5 [55.0-76.0] years; 192 [32.9%] females), new-onset or worsening AKI within 7 postoperative days occurred in 22.8% (66/290) randomized to receive dobutamine plus norepinephrine vs 34.7% (102/294) randomized to receive norepinephrine alone (adjusted risk ratio [ARR], 0.64 [95% CI, 0.49-0.83]). No significant differences were observed in 9 of the 11 secondary outcomes. SOFA scores on postoperative day 1 (adjusted difference, -0.53 [95% CI, -0.98 to -0.07]) were lower and urine output 1 hour post intervention (adjusted difference, 0.55 [95% CI, 0.03 to 1.07] mL/kg/h) was higher in the dobutamine plus norepinephrine group. Stage 2 and 3 AKI were lower in the dobutamine plus norepinephrine group compared with the norepinephrine alone group (stage 2: 4.8% vs 9.9%; ARR, 0.48 [95% CI, 0.26-0.88]; stage 3: 7.9% vs 13.6%; ARR, 0.56 [95% CI, 0.35-0.91]). Tachycardia (heart rate >100/min) occurred more frequently in patients receiving dobutamine and norepinephrine than norepinephrine alone. Among adult patients with septic shock undergoing surgical source control, intraoperative dobutamine combined with norepinephrine reduced the incidence of new-onset or worsening AKI within 7 postoperative days compared with norepinephrine. articles.title: SGLT2 Inhibitors Reduce Heart Failure Hospitalization, Cardiovascular Death and Kidney Outcomes in Type 2 Diabetes: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
articles.abstract: Cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease are the principal drivers of morbidity and mortality in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) have demonstrated cardiorenal benefits in landmark trials, yet cross-trial inconsistencies in cardiovascular mortality, renal endpoints and drug-specific effects leave the class-level estimates incompletely synthesized. PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus and CENTRAL were searched from inception through 15 May 2026. Large placebo-controlled RCTs (≥ 1000 participants) and prespecified subgroup analyses in adults with T2DM were eligible. The primary outcome was the composite of first hospitalization for heart failure (HHF) or cardiovascular death (CV death). Secondary outcomes were 3-point major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), CV DEATH, myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, first HHF and composite kidney outcomes. Hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using random-effects inverse-variance models. Fourteen studies (76 969 patients; 41 761 SGLT2i, 35 208 placebo) were included. SGLT2i reduced the primary composite by 23% (HR: 0.77, 95% CI: 0.73-0.81, p < 0.0001; I = 0%), with no effect modification by baseline HF (p-interaction = 0.82) or established ASCVD (p-interaction = 0.46). MACE was reduced by 14% (HR: 0.86, 95% CI: 0.81-0.92), driven by significant reductions in CV DEATH (HR: 0.86, 95% CI: 0.79-0.93) and MI (HR: 0.88, 95% CI: 0.81-0.96), with no significant effect on stroke (HR: 0.93, 95% CI: 0.81-1.08). First, HHF was reduced by 29% (HR: 0.71, 95% CI: 0.66-0.77) and composite kidney outcomes by 31% (HR: 0.69, 95% CI: 0.60-0.79). SGLT2i confer consistent and clinically meaningful cardiorenal protection in T2DM across the full spectrum of cardiovascular and renal risk. The ertugliflozin estimate and the moderate heterogeneity in kidney outcomes should be interpreted in the context of trial-level clinical differences and nonstandardized kidney endpoint definitions. These findings support proactive, guideline-concordant initiation of evidence-based SGLT2i agents by endocrinologists, cardiologists and primary care providers as foundational therapy in T2DM.

articles.title: Petrelintide, a human amylin analogue for the treatment of obesity (ZUPREME 1): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial.
articles.abstract: Petrelintide is a novel, long-acting amylin analogue being developed for long-term treatment of obesity, leveraging a mechanism of action distinct from incretin-based treatments. This phase 2 trial aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of once-weekly petrelintide versus placebo in people with obesity. This multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial involved 32 sites (public hospitals and private clinics) in Poland, Romania, and the USA. Adults aged at least 18 years without type 2 diabetes, with a BMI of at least 30 kg/m or with a BMI of at least 27 kg/m with hypertension or dyslipidaemia, or both, were randomly assigned (5:1) to self-administered subcutaneous injections of once-weekly maintenance doses of petrelintide (1·0-9·0 mg) or placebo for 42 weeks including dose escalation. Randomisation was done via a central interactive response technology system and was stratified by MRI participation. Participants, trial staff, and the study funder were masked to treatment assignment but not to different maintenance doses; masking was maintained by use of identical vials for petrelintide and placebo. The primary endpoint was percentage change in bodyweight from baseline after 28 weeks. Analyses included all randomly assigned participants who received at least one dose. Missing data were assumed to be missing at random. The trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06662539) and the Clinical Trials Information System (2024-512549-18) and was completed on Mar 7, 2026. From Dec 9, 2024, to Feb 25, 2025, we screened 714 participants, of whom 493 were randomly assigned and 485 received at least one dose of petrelintide or placebo. 79 participants received at least one dose of treatment with petrelintide 1·0 mg, 81 with petrelintide 2·5 mg, 83 with petrelintide 5·0 mg, 79 with petrelintide 7·0 mg, 82 with petrelintide 9·0 mg, and 81 with placebo. 255 (53%) participants were female, 230 (47%) were male, mean age was 47 (SD 12) years, mean bodyweight 107·1 kg (20·3), mean BMI 36·7 kg/m (5·5), and 419 (86%) were White. Mean percentage change in bodyweight from baseline after 28 weeks (efficacy estimand) was -7·9% (95% CI -9·0 to -6·7) with petrelintide 1·0 mg, -7·9% (-9·0 to -6·7) with petrelintide 2·5 mg, -9·8% (-10·9 to -8·6) with petrelintide 5·0 mg, -9·3% (-10·5 to -8·2) with petrelintide 7·0 mg, and -9·4% (-10·5 to -8·3) with petrelintide 9·0 mg versus -1·7% (-2·8 to -0·5) with placebo. Estimated treatment differences versus placebo were -6·2% (-7·9 to -4·5) with petrelintide 1·0 mg, -6·2% (-7·8 to -4·5) with petrelintide 2·5 mg, -8·1% (-9·7 to -6·5) with petrelintide 5·0 mg, -7·7% (-9·3 to -6·0) with petrelintide 7·0 mg, and -7·7% (-9·4 to -6·1) with petrelintide 9·0 mg. Bodyweight continued to decline to week 42, with reductions of up to -10·7% with petrelintide. The most common adverse event with petrelintide was nausea (79 [20%] of 404 participants vs five [6%] participants with placebo). Vomiting was infrequent with petrelintide (12 [3%] participants vs five [6%] with placebo); active treatment and placebo had similarly low rates for diarrhoea (30 [7%] participants vs six [7%] with placebo) and constipation (28 [7%] vs three [4%] with placebo). No deaths were reported. Petrelintide achieved clinically meaningful weight reduction and had similar gastrointestinal tolerability to that of placebo apart from predominantly mild nausea during dose escalation, supporting further evaluation as a long-term obesity therapy. articles.title: Continuous Glucose Monitoring in Non-Insulin-Treated Type 2 Diabetes.
articles.abstract: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) has been shown to be beneficial in persons with type 1 diabetes and others with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, but its role in the treatment of persons with type 2 diabetes not being treated with insulin has needed further study. articles.title: Long-Acting HIV Therapy in African Adults with Adherence Challenges.
articles.abstract: In eastern and southern Africa, approximately 1 million people living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and receiving oral therapy do not have viral suppression because of adherence challenges. We conducted a phase 3b, open-label, randomized trial to compare long-acting injectable cabotegravir plus rilpivirine with oral dolutegravir-based therapy among adults with virally suppressed HIV type 1 (viral load, <200 copies per milliliter) and suboptimal adherence or care engagement. The participants were assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive intramuscular injections of cabotegravir (600 mg) plus rilpivirine (900 mg) every 8 weeks, with the first two injection visits occurring 4 weeks apart, or to continue daily oral dolutegravir-based therapy; baseline drug-resistance testing was not performed. The primary end point was a viral load of less than 50 copies per milliliter at week 48; noninferiority was assessed with a margin of -10 percentage points. Confirmed virologic failure (two consecutive viral loads of ≥200 copies per milliliter) was a key secondary end point. A total of 540 participants were enrolled across seven sites in Kenya, South Africa, and Uganda; 537 were included in the primary analysis. At 48 weeks, 244 of 268 participants (91.0%) in the long-acting-therapy group had a viral load of less than 50 copies per milliliter, as compared with 240 of 269 participants (89.2%) in the oral-therapy group (risk difference, 1.9 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -3.1 to 6.9), which met the criterion for noninferiority. The results of a per-protocol analysis were consistent with those of the primary analysis. Confirmed virologic failure occurred in 5 participants (1.9%) in the long-acting-therapy group and in no participants in the oral-therapy group (risk difference, 1.9 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.3 to 3.5). Serious adverse events were reported in 11 of 271 participants (4.1%) who received long-acting therapy and in 8 of 269 participants (3.0%) who received oral therapy (risk difference, 1.1 percentage points; 95% CI, -1.1 to 4.2). Among persons with HIV in Africa who have adherence challenges, long-acting cabotegravir plus rilpivirine was noninferior to oral dolutegravir-based therapy for maintaining a viral load of less than 50 copies per milliliter. articles.title: Regimens of vitamin D supplementation for women during pregnancy.
articles.abstract: Vitamin D deficiency is common in pregnancy and has been associated with adverse health outcomes for the mother and infant, including pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, preterm birth, and low birthweight. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a vitamin D intake of 200 international units (IU) per day during pregnancy. Vitamin D supplementation is recommended for women with suspected vitamin D deficiency, but it is not universally recommended. The effects of different doses (regimens) of vitamin D during pregnancy have not been established. This is an update of a Cochrane review first published in 2019, which concluded that vitamin D supplementation (at any dose) may have little or no beneficial effects on maternal or neonatal outcomes. To assess the effects of different doses of vitamin D supplementation (alone or in combination with calcium or other micronutrients) during pregnancy: more than 600 IU/day versus up to 600 IU/day, and 4000 IU/day or more versus less than 4000 IU/day. We searched the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), ClinicalTrials.gov, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, and relevant databases in April 2026. We included randomised trials evaluating the effects of different vitamin D regimens during pregnancy on maternal and infant health outcomes. Trials of pregnant women with pre-existing conditions or multiple pregnancies were excluded. The critical maternal outcomes were pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, and any adverse events. The critical infant outcomes were preterm birth and low birthweight. We used the Cochrane RoB 1 tool to independently assess the risk of bias in included studies. Two review authors independently assessed study eligibility and extracted data from included studies. We conducted fixed-effect meta-analyses in RevMan where it was reasonable to assume that studies were estimating the same underlying treatment effect. If substantial heterogeneity was detected, we conducted random-effects meta-analyses, using the Mantel-Haenszel method for dichotomous outcomes and inverse-variance method for continuous outcomes. We used the GRADE approach to assess the certainty of the evidence. This review update included 25 studies with 7008 pregnant women. The included studies were conducted in 14 countries between 2004 and 2024. We excluded 29 studies, identified 23 ongoing studies, and listed 21 studies as awaiting classification. The overall risk of bias of the 25 included studies was mixed. The certainty of the evidence was low for most critical outcomes due to serious risk of bias and imprecision in the results. Vitamin D at a dose of more than 600 IU/day versus up to 600 IU/day, alone or in combination with other micronutrients (19 studies, 5141 women) Vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy at doses of more than 600 IU/day, compared with up to 600 IU/day, may make little or no difference to the risk of pre-eclampsia (risk ratio (RR) 0.90, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.65 to 1.25; 8 studies, 2629 women; low-certainty evidence), gestational diabetes (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.40; 6 studies, 2373 women; low-certainty evidence), preterm birth (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.32; 7 studies, 3411 women; low-certainty evidence), or low birthweight (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.14; 6 studies, 2090 women; low-certainty evidence). Vitamin D at a dose of 4000 IU/day or more versus less than 4000 IU/day, alone or in combination with other micronutrients (14 studies, 4954 women) Vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy at doses of 4000 IU/day or more, compared with less than 4000 IU/day, may make little or no difference to the risk of pre-eclampsia (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.25; 5 studies, 2456 women; low-certainty evidence), gestational diabetes (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.35; 5 studies, 2420 women; low-certainty evidence), or preterm birth (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.19; 7 studies, 3409 women; low-certainty evidence), and probably makes little or no difference to the risk of low birthweight (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.21; 3 studies, 1637 women; moderate-certainty evidence). Adverse events in both comparisons Reporting of adverse events (e.g. hypercalcaemia, hypervitaminosis D) was heterogeneous across studies. Few adverse events were reported, and we observed no differences between groups (low-certainty to moderate-certainty evidence). Vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy at higher versus lower doses may make little or no difference to the risk of pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, preterm birth, or low birthweight. Future research should prioritise adequately powered trials with harmonised study designs that include more women from under-represented regions and focus on a consistently defined set of maternal and infant health outcomes. Additionally, trials should include longer follow-up to assess infant and child health outcomes beyond birth. This Cochrane review had no dedicated funding. The previous version of this review was published in 2019 (DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD013446). The original protocol for this review was registered with PROSPERO (https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42018103763).

articles.title: Acute aortic syndrome rule-out criteria: development and external validation.
articles.abstract: Acute aortic syndrome (AAS) is a rare but catastrophic event, presenting with non-specific symptoms that mimic common conditions, and carries a mortality approaching 80% when missed. Current clinical tools, including the Aortic Dissection Detection Risk Score (ADD-RS) and its refinement, the simplified AORTA score, achieve high sensitivity when combined with D-dimer but fail to identify a population at sufficiently low risk to safely avoid further testing. To address this gap, the Acute Aortic Syndrome Rule-Out Criteria (ARC) were developed and validated, a pragmatic bedside tool designed to safely exclude AAS in low-risk patients without additional testing. A retrospective multistep derivation and validation study was conducted. The derivation cohort included patients with confirmed AAS from the International Registry of Acute Aortic Dissection (IRAD). Starting from existing scores, candidate predictors were identified from the IRAD dataset and sequentially added to achieve sensitivity ≥ 99%. External validation was performed in patients with suspected AAS across three prospective multicentre cohorts (ADvISED, PROFUNDUS, and DAShED). Diagnostic accuracy was assessed using sensitivity and specificity with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The final seven-variable ARC included age >60 years, abrupt onset pain, severe pain, hypotension/shock, neurological deficit, pulse deficit, and known aortic disease. Patients were classified as positive if any ARC variable was present and negative only if all variables were absent. In the derivation cohort, ARC achieved a sensitivity of 99.2% (95% CI 99.1-99.3). In the ADvISED/PROFUNDUS cohort (4598 patients, 10.2% AAS prevalence), sensitivity was 100% (95% CI 99.2-100) with specificity 23.7% (95% CI 22.4-25.0). In the DAShED cohort (5346 patients, 0.3% prevalence), sensitivity was 100% (95% CI 76.8-100) and specificity 36.4% (95% CI 35.1-37.7), ruling out 36.3% of patients without missing any AAS cases. ARC is an externally validated, pragmatic clinical rule demonstrating high diagnostic sensitivity in a large external validation cohort. When incorporated into existing diagnostic pathways, ARC has the potential to reduce unnecessary testing while maintaining diagnostic performance. Further prospective validation is required to confirm its clinical utility.

articles.title: Survival After Risk-Reducing Mastectomy in Patients With Pathogenic Variants in BRCA1 and BRCA2: A Network Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: The independent survival benefit of risk-reducing mastectomy (RRM), separate from risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy (RRSO), remains uncertain among patients with pathogenic variants (PVs) in BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. To evaluate the association of RRM, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based screening, and mammography alone with all-cause and breast cancer-specific mortality using RRSO-adjusted estimates. MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science were searched from January 1, 1990, to May 28, 2026. Search structures, subject headings, and keywords were tailored to each database. Inclusion criteria were English-language prospective and retrospective observational studies of adult female patients with PV or likely PV in BRCA1 and BRCA2 who underwent RRM or breast cancer screening (MRI-based with or without mammography, or mammography alone), with RRSO excluded by design or adjusted for in multivariable analysis. Studies including females with prior breast or ovarian cancer were excluded. Study reporting followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 network meta-analysis extension. Two authors independently performed study selection, data extraction, and bias assessment using a risk-of-bias assessment tool (ROBINS-I V2) and a grading approach (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation [GRADE]). Frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis was performed with surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) estimation. Sensitivity analysis was conducted for the BRCA1 cohort. Primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcome was breast cancer-specific mortality. All outcomes were analyzed and reported as hazard ratios (HRs) with corresponding 95% CIs. Five observational studies with 7937 female patients (median [range] age, 35.9 [unreported] years to 43.4 [32.0-55.7] years) met the inclusion criteria. RRM was associated with lower all-cause mortality compared with MRI-based screening (HR, 0.37; 95% CI, 0.22-0.63) and mammography alone (HR, 0.16; 95% CI, 0.08-0.32). RRM was also associated with lower breast cancer-specific mortality compared with mammography alone (HR, 0.07; 95% CI, 0.01-0.44) but did not have significantly lower mortality than MRI-based screening (HR, 0.26; 95% CI, 0.05-1.35). In BRCA1-only analyses, RRM was associated with lower breast cancer-specific mortality compared with MRI-based screening (HR, 0.13; 95% CI, 0.03-0.66) and mammography alone (HR, 0.03; 95% CI, 0.00-0.15). SUCRA rankings indicated RRM had the highest likelihood of association with the lowest all-cause mortality (SUCRA value, 99.9%). Risk of bias was critical for 4 studies, and certainty of evidence was rated as very low for all 5 studies. In this systematic review and network meta-analysis of RRSO-adjusted analyses, RRM was associated with lower all-cause mortality compared with breast cancer screening among females with PVs in BRCA1 and BRCA2, with the greatest magnitude of association for breast cancer-specific mortality observed in BRCA1 PV carriers. These findings provide less confounded survival estimates to support individualized shared decision-making for RRM.

articles.title: Interleukin-6 Inhibition with Ziltivekimab for Atherosclerotic Disease.
articles.abstract: The inflammatory cytokine interleukin-6 is hypothesized to be a therapeutic target for patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease. Whether neutralizing interleukin-6 levels with ziltivekimab, a monoclonal antibody, reduces the risk of adverse cardiovascular events remains unknown. We conducted a multinational, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial involving adults with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, and cardiovascular inflammation (defined by a high-sensitivity C-reactive protein [CRP] level of ≥2 mg per liter). Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive subcutaneous ziltivekimab (15 mg once monthly) or placebo. The primary efficacy end point was a 3-point major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE). This composite end point included death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke. A total of 6376 patients were included in the full analysis population: 3184 were assigned to receive ziltivekimab and 3192 to receive placebo. The mean age of the patients was 69.4 years, and 27.5% were women. At 24 months, the between-group difference in the median percent change in the levels of inflammatory biomarkers among patients receiving ziltivekimab as compared with those receiving placebo was -76 percentage points for free interleukin-6 and -64 percentage points for high-sensitivity CRP. During a median follow-up of 33 months, a primary end-point event occurred in 561 patients (17.6%) in the ziltivekimab group and in 565 patients (17.7%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.99; 95% confidence interval, 0.88 to 1.11; P = 0.84). Serious adverse events occurred in 54.6% of the patients in the ziltivekimab group and in 54.8% of those in the placebo group; serious infections occurred in 20.4% and 17.9%, respectively. Among patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, and cardiovascular inflammation, a strategy of lowering interleukin-6 levels with ziltivekimab did not result in a lower risk of cardiovascular events than placebo. (Funded by Novo Nordisk; ZEUS ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05021835.).

articles.title: Long-Term Survival After Initial Invasive or Conservative Management of Stable Coronary Disease in ISCHEMIA-EXTEND.
articles.abstract: It is unknown whether routine invasive management of chronic coronary disease improves long-term survival when added to guideline-directed medical therapy. To compare the effects of initial invasive and conservative strategies on long-term mortality in patients with chronic coronary disease. In this long-term follow-up study of the International Study of Comparative Health Effectiveness with Medical and Invasive Approaches (ISCHEMIA), an international trial of patients with chronic coronary disease, moderate or severe ischemia, left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% or more, and no left main coronary artery disease, unacceptable angina, or recent acute coronary syndrome, participants were randomized at 320 sites in 37 countries beginning August 2012 and followed up through December 2025. Data were analyzed using the intention-to-treat principle. ISCHEMIA randomized patients to an initial invasive strategy of guideline-directed medical therapy plus coronary angiography and revascularization (when feasible) or an initial conservative strategy with guideline-directed medical therapy alone, with invasive management for failure of medical therapy. All-cause, cardiovascular, and noncardiovascular mortality were analyzed using cumulative incidence estimates, Cox and Fine-Gray models, bayesian analysis, and restricted mean survival time. Among 5179 participants, median age was 64 (IQR, 58-70) years; 23% were female, 42% had diabetes, and median ejection fraction was 60% (IQR, 55%-65%). During 9-year median follow-up (range, 1 day to 13.4 years), 1071 deaths occurred (782 during extended follow-up): 672 cardiovascular, 359 noncardiovascular, and 40 unclassified. All-cause 11-year mortality was not significantly different between groups (25.8% invasive vs 26.9% conservative; estimated difference, -1.0 percentage point [95% CI, -4.2 to 2.1 percentage points]; adjusted hazard ratio [AHR], 0.97 [95% CI, 0.86-1.09]). By bayesian analysis, the posterior probability of more than 1 percentage-point survival benefit to invasive vs conservative was low (18%). Cardiovascular mortality at 11 years was 15.8% in the invasive group vs 17.1% in the conservative group (estimated difference, -1.4 percentage points [95% CI, -4.0 to 1.3 percentage points]; AHR, 0.88 [95% CI, 0.75-1.02]). Noncardiovascular mortality at 11 years was 9.1% in the invasive group vs 8.1% in the conservative group (estimated difference, 1.0 percentage point [95% CI, -0.9 to 2.9 percentage points]; AHR, 1.18 [95% CI, 0.96-1.45]). Eleven-year restricted mean survival was not significantly different (estimated difference, 14 days [95% CI, -41 to 70 days]). In this study, long-term all-cause mortality in patients with high-risk chronic coronary disease was not significantly different after routine invasive vs initial conservative management. articles.title: Discontinuing Statins in Older Adults without Cardiovascular Disease.
articles.abstract: Whether discontinuing statin therapy in older adults with at least two chronic conditions but no known cardiovascular disease affects the time to a first cardiovascular event is not well characterized. We conducted an international, open-label, randomized, controlled trial that enrolled adults at least 70 years of age who were taking statins for primary prevention. Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either discontinue or continue statin therapy and other lipid-lowering therapies. The primary outcome was a composite of nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal ischemic stroke, or death from any cause, whichever occurred first. The primary analysis assessed noninferiority on the basis of the between-group difference in restricted mean event-free survival time at 2 years, with a noninferiority margin of -5.2 weeks. A total of 1880 participants underwent randomization: 938 were assigned to the discontinuation group and 942 to the continuation group. The mean age of the participants was 77.5 years, and 46.9% were women. The between-group difference in the restricted mean event-free survival time at 2 years was -2.0 weeks (95% confidence interval, -3.7 to -0.3; P<0.001 for noninferiority). Over a median follow-up of 103 weeks, 119 participants (12.7%) in the discontinuation group and 87 (9.2%) in the continuation group had a primary-outcome event. At least one serious adverse event occurred in 43.0% of the participants in the discontinuation group and in 39.8% in the continuation group. Among older adults with at least two chronic conditions but no known cardiovascular disease, discontinuation of statin therapy was noninferior to continuation with respect to major cardiovascular events or death from any cause at 2 years. (Funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation; STREAM ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05178420.).

articles.title: Ganaplacide plus lumefantrine solid dispersion formulation for children with uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria (KALUMI): an open-label, multicentre, randomised, controlled, adaptive, phase 2, non-inferiority trial.
articles.abstract: Ganaplacide plus lumefantrine solid dispersion formulation (SDF) is a novel antimalarial combination shown to be effective and well tolerated in adults, adolescents, and children with uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Here, we aimed to assess food effects on drug exposure and non-inferiority of ganaplacide plus lumefantrine SDF to artemether-lumefantrine. This open-label, multicentre, randomised, controlled, adaptive, phase 2, non-inferiority trial was conducted at ten clinics and hospitals in Burkina Faso, Mali, Côte d'Ivoire, Gabon, and DR Congo. Eligible patients had microscopically confirmed uncomplicated P falciparum malaria. In run-in cohorts 1 and 2, patients (aged 12 years to <18 years with bodyweight ≥35·0 kg) were randomly assigned (1:1) to dosing in the fed group (standard meal 400-500 calories, with 20-30 g of fat) or in the fasted group. Patients received ganaplacide 400 mg plus lumefantrine SDF 240 mg (run-in cohort 1) and ganaplacide 400 mg plus lumefantrine SDF 480 mg (run-in cohort 2) once per day for 2 days. In the main part (cohort 1 [age 2 years to <12 years] and cohort 2 [age 6 months to <2 years]), patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to ganaplacide plus lumefantrine SDF (at the dose regimen selected from run-in cohorts, adjusted by bodyweight) or artemether-lumefantrine for 3 days. Randomisation, using an Interactive response technology system, was stratified by age group and country (cohort 1) or by country (run-in cohorts and cohort 2). Food effects on the bioavailability of ganaplacide and lumefantrine were assessed in run-in cohorts. The primary endpoint for the main part of the study was PCR-corrected adequate clinical and parasitological response on day 29 in the per protocol population. The non-inferiority margin was 10%. Safety and tolerability was a secondary endpoint. This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04546633 (completed). Between Feb 16, 2021, and July 14, 2024, 577 patients were screened and 282 were ineligible. 51 patients were enrolled in run-in cohort 1, 24 in run-in cohort 2, and 220 in the main part (110 each assigned to ganaplacide plus lumefantrine SDF or artemether-lumefantrine). Two (4%) patients discontinued early in run-in cohort 1 and all 24 in run-in cohort 2 completed the study. Across run-in cohorts 1 and 2, the food effect on ganaplacide was small (mean fed:fasted ratios from 0·98 to 1·41), but a significant food effect was observed for lumefantrine (mean ratios ranging from 1·48 to 2·87). Ganaplacide 400 mg plus lumefantrine SDF 480 mg given once per day for 3 days with a light meal (100-300 calories, with 5-10 g of fat) was selected as the full dose and 206 (94%) of 220 patients completed the main part. For PCR-corrected adequate clinical and parasitological response on day 29, response rates were 97 (99% [95% CI 94 to 100]) of 98 in the ganaplacide plus lumefantrine SDF group and 98 (99% [95 to 100]) of 99 in the artemether-lumefantrine group (treatment difference -0·0% [-2·9 to 2·8]), with the lower limit of 95% CI above -10%. The most common adverse events were vomiting (32 [29%] of 110 in the ganaplacide plus lumefantrine SDF group vs 12 [11%] of 110 in the artemether-lumefantrine group) and hypokalaemia (27 [25%] vs 16 [15%]). Ganaplacide 400 mg plus lumefantrine SDF 480 mg once per day for 3 days with a light meal was non-inferior to artemether-lumefantrine for patients with uncomplicated P falciparum malaria. This regimen was further evaluated in a phase 3 trial (NCT05842954). articles.title: Long-Term Survival After Initial Invasive or Conservative Management of Stable Coronary Disease in Patients With Advanced Chronic Kidney Disease: ISCHEMIA-CKD EXTEND.
articles.abstract: In the ISCHEMIA-CKD trial (International Study of Comparative Health Effectiveness With Medical and Invasive Approaches-Chronic Kidney Disease), at a median follow-up of 2.2 years, the primary composite outcome of death or nonfatal myocardial infarction was similar between an initial invasive strategy (INV) compared with an initial conservative strategy (CON) in patients with moderate or severe myocardial ischemia and advanced chronic kidney disease. However, the long-term outcomes comparing the 2 strategies are unknown. Participants in the ISCHEMIA-CKD trial were randomly assigned to either INV, involving coronary angiography and revascularization when feasible, added to guideline-directed medical therapy or to CON with guideline-directed medical therapy alone and invasive procedures reserved for failure of guideline-directed medical therapy. After the active intervention trial phase, long-term vital status follow-up was conducted through participant contact by participating sites and by health record and centralized death database searches. The primary outcome for the extended follow-up phase was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes were cause-specific mortality, including cardiovascular and noncardiovascular mortality. Among the 777 participants randomized (388 to INV and 389 to CON), over a median of 8 years of follow-up, vital status retention among survivors was 95%. There was a total of 429 deaths (55%). Cumulative all-cause mortality (57.4% versus 56.8%; adjusted hazard ratio, 1.05 [95% CI, 0.87-1.28]) or cardiovascular mortality (40.3% versus 38.4%; adjusted hazard ratio, 1.06 [95% CI, 0.84-1.34]) at 8 years did not differ between INV and CON. The restricted mean survival time was 1941 days (1834-2047 days) for INV versus 1990 days (1885-2094 days) for CON, with an adjusted estimated difference of -99 days (-245 to 46). The posterior probability of at least a 1 percentage point lower or higher death with INV at the 8-year median follow-up was 28% and 52%, respectively. Similarly, the posterior probability of at least a 1 percentage point lower or higher cardiovascular mortality with INV was 23% and 56%, respectively. In patients with at least moderate ischemia and advanced chronic kidney disease, there was no significant long-term benefit of an initial INV at reducing the risk of all-cause or cardiovascular mortality compared with an initial conservative strategy. articles.title: Orforglipron for Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Results From 2 Randomized Clinical Trials (ATTAIN-OSA).
articles.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a common disorder characterized by repeated upper airway collapse during sleep that is associated with reduced quality of life and increased incidence of cardiometabolic disease. To assess the effects of orforglipron on moderate to severe OSA in adults with obesity or overweight, compared with placebo. Two 52-week, phase 3, multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized clinical trials were conducted at 66 sites in the US, Argentina, Brazil, China, Czech Republic, Germany, Japan, Mexico, and Taiwan. Adults with moderate to severe OSA and body mass index (BMI; calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) of 27 or higher were enrolled between November 11, 2024, and July 23, 2025. Final follow-up occurred on July 30, 2026. Trial 1 included patients not receiving positive airway pressure treatment and trial 2 included patients receiving positive airway pressure treatment. Patients were randomized (1:1) to receive either once-daily orforglipron (maximum tolerated dose: equivalent to 9-, 14.5-, or 17.2-mg tablet dose) or placebo. The primary end point was change in apnea-hypopnea index (AHI, events/h) from baseline to week 52. Seven key multiplicity-controlled secondary end points included change in sleep apnea-specific hypoxic burden, the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Short Form Sleep-Related Impairment T-score, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein. A total of 363 patients were randomized in trial 1 (mean age, 48.4 years; BMI, 37.4; AHI, 50.7 events/h; 31.4% female) and 349 patients were randomized in trial 2 (mean age, 51.1 years; BMI, 38.6; AHI, 57.6 events/h; 26.9% female). For the treatment regimen estimand, in trial 1, the mean AHI change was -17.8 for orforglipron compared with -4.5 for placebo (difference, -13.2 [95% CI, -17.7 to -8.7]; P < .001) at 52 weeks. In trial 2, the mean AHI change was -17.3 for orforglipron and -5.3 for placebo (difference, -12.0 [95% CI, -17.1 to -6.9]; P < .001) at 52 weeks. Of 7 key secondary end points, 6 were statistically significant, favoring orforglipron. Gastrointestinal events were the most commonly reported adverse events, occurring in 123 (68.0%) participants randomized to receive orforglipron vs 68 (37.4%) randomized to receive placebo in trial 1 and in 125 (70.6%) participants randomized to receive orforglipron vs 63 (36.6%) randomized to receive placebo in trial 2. These results provide evidence for the potential use of oral orforglipron to improve sleep-disordered breathing in adults with moderate to severe OSA and obesity or overweight. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06649045.

structuredAbstract.text: A total of 363 patients were randomized in trial 1 (mean age, 48.4 years; BMI, 37.4; AHI, 50.7 events/h; 31.4% female) and 349 patients were randomized in trial 2 (mean age, 51.1 years; BMI, 38.6; AHI, 57.6 events/h; 26.9% female). For the treatment regimen estimand, in trial 1, the mean AHI change was -17.8 for orforglipron compared with -4.5 for placebo (difference, -13.2 [95% CI, -17.7 to -8.7]; P < .001) at 52 weeks. In trial 2, the mean AHI change was -17.3 for orforglipron and -5.3 for placebo (difference, -12.0 [95% CI, -17.1 to -6.9]; P < .001) at 52 weeks. Of 7 key secondary end points, 6 were statistically significant, favoring orforglipron. Gastrointestinal events were the most commonly reported adverse events, occurring in 123 (68.0%) participants randomized to receive orforglipron vs 68 (37.4%) randomized to receive placebo in trial 1 and in 125 (70.6%) participants randomized to receive orforglipron vs 63 (36.6%) randomized to receive placebo in trial 2.

structuredAbstract.label: CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
structuredAbstract.text: These results provide evidence for the potential use of oral orforglipron to improve sleep-disordered breathing in adults with moderate to severe OSA and obesity or overweight.

Closed-Loop Insulin Delivery in Inpatient Care: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Clinical and Implementation Outcomes.
articles.abstract: Closed-loop (CL) insulin delivery systems have transformed outpatient diabetes care. However, evidence supporting their role in inpatient settings is limited. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the safety, efficacy, and implementation of CL systems in inpatient care. This review followed PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO: CRD420251133486). Eligible studies reported glycaemic, safety, and/or implementation outcomes for adults managed with CL systems in inpatient care. EMBASE, PubMed, MEDLINE, Scopus, CINAHL, and Cochrane Library were searched from inception to August 2026. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB2 and ROBINS-I. Random-effects meta-analysis evaluated glycaemic outcomes and length of stay (LOS). Results were presented as pooled mean differences (MDs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Implementation data were analysed thematically. Intrapartum outcomes were analysed separately. Thirteen inpatient studies were included, nine contributing to meta-analysis. CL delivery increased time in range (MD +22.27%, 95% CI: 16.03-28.51; p < 0.001) and reduced time above range (MD -23.75%, 95% CI: -28.05 to -19.45; p < 0.001), mean glucose (MD -1.66 mmol/L, 95% CI: -2.29 to -1.03; p < 0.001) and glucose standard deviation (MD -0.64 mmol/L, 95% CI: -0.85 to -0.43; p < 0.001). No significant differences were observed in time below range, coefficient of variation or LOS. Total daily insulin dose was higher (MD +10.82 IU/day, 95% CI: 0.02-21.62; p = 0.05). No serious device-attributed adverse events were reported. Implementation challenges included staff training, technical support, and workflow integration. Four additional intrapartum studies were included; two contributed to the meta-analysis, showing increased pregnancy-specific time in range (MD +11.82%, 95% CI: 5.56-18.08; p < 0.001). CL systems improve inpatient glycaemic control, although effects on LOS and comparative safety remain uncertain. Wider adoption requires sustainable technical and organisational support.
